chapter_en: The Mitzva of Settling the Land

sections.title_en: A National Mitzva
sections.body_en:
The mitzva of settling the Land is made up of two parts: a general mitzva and a personal mitzva. The general mitzva is placed upon the whole of Israel, and its substance is the conquest of the Land and its settlement by the people of Israel. The personal mitzva obliges every single individual of Israel to live in the Land and to take part in settling it. First we will deal with the first part, that is, with the mitzva placed upon the whole nation to conquer the Land, to rule it and to settle in it. And so wrote the Ramban (Omissions to Sefer Ha-mitzvot, positive mitzva 4): "We were commanded to inherit the land which God, may He be exalted, gave to our forefathers, to Avraham, to Yitzḥak and to Ya'akov, and not to leave it in the hand of others among the nations or to desolation, and this is what is said (Bamidbar 33:53-54): And you shall take possession of the land and dwell in it, for to you I have given the land to possess it. And you shall inherit the land…"

When we examine his words carefully, we find that there are two sides to the general mitzva of settling the Land. One is that the Land should be under the rule of Israel and not under foreign rule. But with the conquest of the Land the mitzva is not yet completed, and one must add the second side, which is to settle the whole Land in practice, so that it does not remain desolate. And it is clear that urban settlement and building houses alone are not enough, since in that way desolate parts would remain in the Land; rather, the mitzva is to make all the desolate places of the Land bloom, so that the blessing of each place is revealed in the best way.

The Ramban emphasised that this mitzva applies in all generations: in every generation Israel is commanded to inherit the Land and settle it, and not only at the time of the conquest of the Land after the Exodus from Egypt. But for many generations we were in a state of duress, for we were in exile, in body and in soul, and we could not fulfil the mitzva. By the kindness of God, in recent generations God has begun to cause our salvation to sprout, our situation has changed, and we are able to fulfil the mitzva.1

notes_en.en:
These foundations were well explained, orally and in writing, by our teacher and master Rav Tzvi Yehuda Ha-kohen Kook zt"l, for example in his essay 'Le-mitzvat Ha-aretz' (Le-netivot Yisrael, Beit El edition, vol. 1, pp. 160-164). He first explained the great importance of the mitzva: it is the only one that overrides a 'shevut', for the Sages permitted buying a house in the Land of Israel from a gentile on Shabbat, as explained in Gittin 8b and Bava Kamma 80b, and in Tosafot there. And this is a great thing, for because of the stringency of Shabbat the Sages made a fence and decreed to cancel the blowing of the shofar and the taking of the lulav when Rosh Ha-shana and the first day of Sukkot fall on Shabbat, even though these are Torah mitzvot (and so in Pesaḥim 92a, and Rambam 6:6). Whereas for the sake of settling the Land the Sages set aside their own words and permitted the prohibition of 'shevut', whose source is an asmakhta; and according to the Semag, instructing a gentile is forbidden by Torah law, see there. He further added, against those who doubt the binding force of the mitzva, that what is brought in Tosafot Ketubot 110b in the name of R. Ḥayim, "that it does not apply in our time", the Maharit (YD 28) and many other great ones among our later rabbis (see Gilyon Maharsha Ketubot there, and Ḥatam Sofer YD 234) have already determined that some mistaken student wrote it. And in the responsa of the Rivash 387 he wrote that the mitzva of settling the Land of Israel is not a mitzva for its time only, but a mitzva that holds forever, and a mitzva and benefit for all Israel. And so wrote the Tashbetz, vol. 3, 288. And the Ratziya added that one cannot divide between the two sides of the mitzva, that is, general sovereignty and personal dwelling, and both are permanent mitzvot. And he proved that the mitzva is from the Torah, for it is impossible that the Sages would permit buying a house in the Land of Israel on Shabbat and transgressing a 'shevut' for the sake of a rabbinic mitzva. Moreover, they said of the mitzva of settling the Land that it is equal to all the mitzvot, and it is impossible to say this of a rabbinic mitzva (and even after the destruction the mitzva is from the Torah, for these words of the Sages were said after the destruction of the Second Temple). And the fact that the Rambam did not count it among the 613 is not because it is beneath the value of the other mitzvot, but because it is above their ordinary value, and therefore it is not counted in their detailed number, as he established in his roots to Sefer Ha-mitzvot, that it is not fitting to count commands that encompass the whole Torah, and as in his words on mitzva 153. And so wrote at length Em Ha-banim Semeḥa chapter 3, sections 7-10: the Rambam did not count the mitzva of settling the Land because it is an encompassing mitzva, as he wrote in his roots; and so wrote many others. And some explain that the Rambam included the mitzva of settling the Land within other mitzvot, such as "you shall utterly destroy them" (Devarim 20:17; Avnei Nezer YD 454:6), in the mitzva to say the blessing of the Land in Birkat Ha-mazon (Rav Yisraeli), in the mitzva of appointing a king (Rav Lior), in the sanctification of the month (Mashmi'a Shalom), in the prohibition of returning to Egypt (Mitzvot Hashem), in the prohibition of handing a slave over to his master who is outside the Land (Rav Ezra Batzri). And in any case it is clear that according to the Rambam there is a great mitzva to live in the Land and guard it, as he wrote in Laws of Kings 5:9-12, Marriage 13:20, that a spouse is compelled to go up to the Land, and in Laws of Slaves 8:9. And in Laws of Idolatry 10:4, on the prohibition of lo teḥonem, and there 10:6, on the prohibition "they shall not dwell in your land". And some say that according to the Rambam this is a rabbinic mitzva (Rashbash and Pe'at Ha-shulḥan), and according to the Megillat Esther, according to the Rambam there is no mitzva to go up to the Land today. But these positions cannot be reconciled with the words of the Sages and the halakhot we mentioned above. And see the book 'Naḥalat Ya'akov' by Rav Ziesberg, pp. 201-246. And see below at the end of the book the explanation of Rav Rabinovitch of the Rambam's view.
In any case, the prevailing view among the Rishonim and Aḥaronim is that the mitzva of settling the Land applies in our time, according to the words of the Ramban and his definitions, as explained in Pitḥei Teshuva EH 75:6. And so our teacher and master the Ratziya used to say, that not a single posek among the Rishonim and Aḥaronim explicitly disputes the Ramban in halakha. (He further said that no halakha is mentioned in the Shulḥan Arukh in the name of the 'Megillat Esther'.) And so wrote the Mabit 1:139; Radbaz 2:115; responsa Me'il Tzedaka 26; responsa Maharam Alshikh 35, 88; Maharshakh 3:35; Maharit 2:20; Shela, Sha'ar Ha-otiyot, letter kuf; the Ḥida, Yosef Ometz 52; Bi'ur Ha-Gra YD 267:161; Pe'at Ha-shulḥan 1, sk 14; responsa Maharam Galanti 67; Ḥatam Sofer YD 233-234; Mor U-ketzi'a 306; Maharam Schick; Sefer Ḥaredim chapter 1 of the mitzvot dependent on the Land; Minḥat Ḥinukh (at the end of the book, of the positive mitzvot that the Ramban counted, 4); responsa Penei Moshe 1:5 and 27; Zera Avraham 56; Petaḥ Ha-devir 3:248; Sedeh Ha-aretz EH 11; responsa Maḥazeh Avraham 2; Rav Kalischer in his book Derishat Tziyon; Rav Mohilever; Rav Yitzḥak Elḥanan of Kovno; the Aderet; Ḥeshek Shlomo (their words are brought in the book Shivat Tziyon); Yeshu'ot Malko YD 66; the Netziv; Arukh Ha-shulḥan YD 267:129-130; Nefesh Ḥaya; Ḥafetz Ḥayim in Sefer Ha-mitzvot Ha-katzar, negative 192; Rav Ḥayim Palagi; Or Same'aḥ; Ḥazon Ish Shevi'it 24:1, and letter 175; Ḥelkat Ya'akov and others (from 'Naḥalat Ya'akov' p. 67; see there for more sources).

sections.title_en: The Individual's Share in the General Mitzva
sections.body_en:
There are levels upon levels in the share of each individual in the general mitzva of settling the Land. Every Jew who lives in the Land of Israel is a partner in the mitzva of settling the Land, for through his dwelling the hold of the people of Israel on its Land is strengthened. And one who goes to live in relatively desolate places, such as the Negev and the Arava, has a greater share in the mitzva of settling the Land, for through his dwelling the Land is settled and is not left to desolation. And so too one who settles in areas where Arab citizens threaten Israeli sovereignty, such as for example in the Galil, has a greater share in the mitzva.

And one who settles in Yehuda and Shomron fulfils by his dwelling a greater mitzva, because his dwelling makes a double contribution: first, in strengthening the rule of Israel in places that the Arabs want to rob from us; second, for the sake of making the desolation bloom. And the more the settlement is in a place more desolate of Jews, and the more our enemies strive to conquer it, the greater the mitzva of those who live in it. And the Sages have already said (Berakhot 5a): the Land of Israel is acquired through sufferings, and according to the pain is the reward (Avot 5:23).

Beyond this, we have learned that the mitzva of settling the Land must be fulfilled gradually (below 13), and the most sanctified places come first; and Yehuda and Shomron are the most sanctified, for in them the prophecies were revealed to the forefathers and the prophets, and in them the Mishkan of Shilo and the Temple in Jerusalem stood, and therefore the olim from Bavel strove to take hold of them first. Similarly, when God revealed Himself to Ya'akov our forefather in Beit El, which is near Jerusalem, He said to him (Bereshit 28:13-14): "The land on which you lie, to you I will give it and to your seed… and you shall spread abroad to the west and to the east and to the north and to the south, and in you and in your seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed." So from the centre of the Land one must spread out to the expanses of the Land.

The mitzva of settling the Land is unique of its kind, in that by the very fact that a Jew lives in a place of settlement value he fulfils a mitzva. For in all other mitzvot one must perform an act in order to fulfil them, for example: to put on tefillin, to give tzedaka, to pray; but in the mitzva of settling the Land the very dwelling is a mitzva. It follows that for everyone who merits to live in the Land of Israel, and even more in the settlements of Yehuda and Shomron, his routine life, such as eating, sleeping and even every single breath, becomes a reality of mitzva.

Even those who live outside the Land and donate money for the sake of settlement in the Land of Israel, or take part in investments for the development of the economy and science in the Land, are partners to a certain extent in the general mitzva of settling the Land; but they are partners in the mitzva with their money and do not fulfil the mitzva with their bodies. And so too residents of the Land who support the settlements of Yehuda and Shomron are partners in the general mitzva of settling those sanctified places, and according to the measure of their support is the greatness of their mitzva.

sections.title_en: The Mitzva for the Individual to Dwell in It
sections.body_en:
In addition to the general mitzva, that the Land be under the sovereignty of Israel, there is a mitzva upon every single Jew to live in the Land of Israel. Therefore, even at a time when the whole Land will be in the hand of Israel and masses of Jews will fill it, from the river of Egypt to the river Perat, there will still be a mitzva upon every Jew to live in the Land. And also at the time when gentiles ruled the Land, and it seemed that there was no chance that the dwelling of one man would help the general mitzva, there was a personal mitzva upon every Jew to live in the Land. As the Sages said (Ketubot 110b): "A person should always dwell in the Land of Israel, even in a city whose majority are idolaters, and not dwell outside the Land, even in a city whose majority are Israel; for whoever dwells in the Land of Israel is like one who has a God, and whoever dwells outside the Land is like one who has no God, as it is said (Vayikra 25:38): to give you the land of Kena'an, to be your God." And so they said in the Tosefta (Avoda Zara 5:2). And so ruled the Rambam (Laws of Kings 5:12): "A person should always dwell in the Land of Israel, even in a city whose majority are gentiles, and not dwell outside the Land, even in a city whose majority are Israel. For whoever goes out of the Land is as though he worships idols."

And so we have learned that even in the period after the destruction of the Second Temple and the failure of the Bar Kokhva revolt, when the Romans ruled the Land with a hard and cruel hand, and many of the people left the Land because of famine and the sword, the position of the Sages was that it is a mitzva to strive to remain in the Land. And so it is told: It happened that Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, Rabbi Matya ben Ḥarash, Rabbi Ḥananya the nephew of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yonatan were going out of the Land, and they reached Platum and remembered the Land of Israel. They lifted their eyes, their tears flowed, and they tore their garments, and recited this verse (Devarim 11:31-32): "And you shall possess it and dwell in it. And you shall observe to do all the statutes and the judgements." They said: "Dwelling in the Land of Israel is equal to all the mitzvot in the Torah," and they turned back and came to the Land of Israel (Sifrei Re'eh 80).

And although when the government was in the hands of foreigners we did not merit to fulfil the general mitzva, that "the Land be in our hands and not in the hand of another nation", nevertheless every Jew who lived in the Land then fulfilled to a certain extent the general mitzva too, because his very dwelling in the Land helped preserve the bond between Israel and its Land despite the long years of exile. In addition, his dwelling in the Land helped continue the expansion of settlement towards Israeli sovereignty. And if he acted and worked deliberately for this goal, as did the disciples of the Gra who went up to the Land with self-sacrifice and built its ruins in order to bring the redemption near, he became a real partner in the general mitzva.2

notes_en.en: Some of the Aḥaronim wanted to say that the mitzva of settling the Land is a mitzva of fulfilment and not of obligation, that is, one who lives in the Land of Israel fulfils a mitzva, but there is no obligation on those who live outside the Land to go up to the Land. And so wrote Igrot Moshe EH vol. 1, end of 102. But that is not the meaning of the mitzva in the words of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim; see the book 'Naḥalat Ya'akov' pp. 277-310. And it is reasonable that the reason most of Israel did not go up to the Land during the period of exile is not because there is no obligation in it, but because they thought they could not fulfil it because of economic and security reasons and the like, and so they are under duress. And although sometimes this excuse was justified, when the king asked the Ḥaver in the book Ha-kuzari why Israel do not return to their land, the Ḥaver answered (2:24): "Indeed, you have found the place of my shame, king of the Khazars. For indeed this is the sin on account of which the promise that God promised for the Second Temple was not fulfilled… had they all answered the call and returned to the Land of Israel with a willing soul; but only some of them answered, and most of them, and the important among them, remained in Bavel, consenting to exile… and therefore God repaid them according to the thought of their hearts, and the divine promises were fulfilled in them only in a limited measure, according to the smallness of their awakening… We too, had we been ready to draw near to the God of our fathers… then He, may He be blessed, would have been our saviour as He saved our fathers in Egypt. Now that it is not so, the things we say in our prayer, "Bow down at His holy mountain"… "Who returns His Shekhina to Tziyon", and the like, are nothing but the speech of the parrot and the chirping of the starling, for without intention of the heart we say these things or their like, as you rightly remarked, prince of the Khazars."

sections.title_en: The Conquest of the Land and Danger to Life
sections.body_en:
We hold as a principle: "and he shall live by them, and not die by them" (Yoma 85b). That is, the Torah was given to a person so that he will live by it, and not die through it. On this basis the famous halakha was established: "danger to life overrides Shabbat". That is, one desecrates Shabbat to save a dangerously ill person. And not only Shabbat is set aside because of danger to life; all the mitzvot of the Torah are set aside because of danger to life. Therefore, if violent gentiles say to one of Israel that he must transgress one of the mitzvot of the Torah or they will kill him, he should transgress and not be killed. Except for three transgressions: idolatry, forbidden relations and bloodshed. For if they say to a person, kill your fellow or we will kill you, he should be killed and not kill. And so if they say to him, worship such-and-such an idol or we will kill you, he should be killed and not transgress, and so too with forbidden relations. But for all the other mitzvot, a person need not give up his life in order to fulfil them (Sanhedrin 74a).

However, all this is said regarding mitzvot of the individual. But the mitzva of settling the Land, which is a mitzva placed upon the whole of Israel, overrides danger to life. For from the very fact that the Torah commanded us to conquer the Land, we learn that lives must be risked in order to fulfil it, for there is no war without losses, and certainly the Torah did not intend that we rely on a miracle. Rather, the mitzva of settling the Land, being a mitzva of all Israel, requires actual self-sacrifice (Minḥat Ḥinukh 425, 604; Mishpat Kohen 143; Igrot Ha-Re'aya vol. 3, 944). And so the people of Israel conducted themselves in the conquest of the Land in the days of Yehoshua and in the days of David, and likewise at the time of establishing the Second Temple and afterwards in the period of the Ḥashmona'i kingdom.

But the matter must be qualified. The principle 'and he shall live by them', and not die by them, applies also to a general mitzva; only, since the mitzva is general, the calculation is that of the whole nation and not of individual soldiers. Therefore, in a situation where there is a high likelihood that we will not succeed in the war, and will lose the inheritances already in our hands, and the life of the nation will hang in the balance, there is no mitzva to open a war to conquer the Land. The Torah is a Torah of life and not a Torah that commands waging a suicidal war. But when there is a high likelihood that we will win, even though it is certain that some of us will lose their lives, we are commanded to conquer the Land, and at the very least to guard what is already in our hands.

It must be noted that a people that is not ready to fight with self-sacrifice for its land exposes its children to mortal danger from its neighbours. For every people that does not succeed in mobilising its children to fight with self-sacrifice for its land and homeland will in the end be conquered, and its sons and daughters will become plunder. Therefore the mitzva to fight for the Land of Israel with self-sacrifice accords with the considerations of saving human life. So one who fights to defend the borders of Israel fulfils two mitzvot: settling the Land and defending Israel.3

notes_en.en: Rav Shlomo Goren explained in 'Torat Ha-medina' pp. 33-34 that the mitzva to fight for the Land while risking the lives of individuals applies when there is a reasonable chance of winning, for it is proven from Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai in Gittin 56a that when he saw there was no chance, he held that one must surrender to the Romans. And so wrote Rav Avraham Shapira, and likewise Rav Lior, as brought in 'Naḥalat Ya'akov' p. 398, note 18, and on pp. 392-422 there is a whole chapter on this, in which poskim who established these foundations are brought. And there he discusses the question whether the mitzva of dwelling in the Land also overrides danger to life. And he concluded that since conquest and dwelling are one mitzva, settlement too requires a readiness to risk lives. And he brought sources for this from Kaftor Va-feraḥ, from the Magen Avraham in his commentary Zayit Ra'anan on Yalkut Shimoni remez 292, and from the Netziv. And so did the first olim conduct themselves, who fell ill with malaria and died and did not leave their settlement, and likewise the settlers of Yehuda and Shomron in dangerous times. And in my humble opinion there is a great difference between conquest and defence on the one hand and settlement on the other. The Torah's mitzva to conquer the Land and settle it applies to the concepts of war and settlement as they are in human nature. Therefore war, which is a time when the people stands for its life to ensure its existence, requires of soldiers a readiness to risk their lives so that the people can live in security. Settlement, by contrast, must take place in ordinary civilian conditions, and it cannot be based on constant existential risk. And although fleeing from settlement may cause retreat, it is not possible to impose on civilians the level of risk required of fighters, but only the level of risk that ordinary brave people take upon themselves for the sake of a livelihood or of exciting trips in places that carry a certain risk. And everything is according to the time and place. In the period of the First Aliya, many dangers lay in wait for a person all over the world; from time to time epidemics, fires, famine and pogroms spread, and consequently the settlers in the Land too were ready to take more risk. Today living conditions have improved and life expectancy has risen, and consequently people are accustomed to risk their lives less in civilian life, that is, for their livelihood and for trips; and consequently the mitzva to take risks in settlement is also according to what is customary at that time among brave people.

sections.title_en: The State of Israel
sections.body_en:
On the 5th of Iyar, in the year five thousand seven hundred and eight by the count we keep from the creation of the world, at the time of the declaration of the State, the people of Israel merited, after two thousand years of exile, to return and fulfil the mitzva of settling the Land. For at the time of the declaration of the State, Israeli sovereignty was applied to parts of the Land of Israel, and thereby we began to fulfil the mitzva that the Land be in our hands and not in the hand of another nation. And although even before the establishment of the State every Jew who lived in the Land fulfilled for himself the personal mitzva of dwelling in the Land, the principal mitzva, which is the general mitzva, that the Land be in our hands and not in the hand of another nation, we had not yet fulfilled. Even at times when many Jews lived in the Land, as long as the Land was under foreign rule, we did not merit to fulfil the general mitzva.

And so we find that the Sages instituted that whoever sees the cities of Yehuda in their destruction should say: "Your holy cities have become a wilderness" and tear his garment. The rule is that even if most of the residents of those cities are Jews, as long as the government is in the hands of gentiles, they are considered destroyed, and one tears on seeing them. And if they were under Israeli sovereignty, even if most of their residents are gentiles, they are not considered destroyed, and one does not tear on seeing them (Beit Yosef and Baḥ OḤ 561, MB 561:2).4

For many generations, out of duress, we could not fulfil the mitzva, because we had no army and weapons that would allow us to conquer our land and maintain rule in it. It follows that the establishment of Israel's military force before the establishment of the State, and its fortification and consolidation in the establishment of the IDF, enable us to fulfil the mitzva. If so, the very existence of the army is a necessary means for fulfilling the mitzva of settling the Land, in addition to the mitzva of saving Israel from the hand of their enemies. And so it will be until repaired days arrive, and the prophecy of Yeshayahu (2:2-4) is fulfilled: "And it shall come to pass in the end of days that the mountain of the Lord's house shall be established at the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills, and all the nations shall flow to it. And many peoples shall go and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, to the house of the God of Ya'akov, and He will teach us of His ways, and we will walk in His paths; for out of Tziyon shall go forth Torah, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And He shall judge between the nations, and shall decide for many peoples; and they shall beat their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more."

notes_en.en: So taught Rav Tzvi Yehuda Ha-kohen Kook zt"l, that on Independence Day we merited to fulfil the mitzva of settling the Land. Once, at an Independence Day gathering in the Merkaz Ha-rav yeshiva, one of the great rabbis expounded that there is great value in the establishment of the State, for since its establishment yeshivot have multiplied, and it is easier for those who keep the Torah to fulfil mitzvot; therefore one should rejoice and thank God for the establishment of the State. And our teacher and master the Ratziya took the trouble to add and emphasise that the very establishment of the State is the great thing, for it is itself the fulfilment of one of the great mitzvot of the Torah. And out of this certainly more mitzvot will be fulfilled, for one mitzva brings another. Not only this, but the establishment of the State and the blooming of the desolate places is a significant stage in the redemption of Israel. As explained in Peninei Halakha Zemanim 4:2, according to the prophets and the Sages, the ingathering of the exiles and the return of sovereignty in the establishment of the State are the beginning of the redemption. In addition, on Independence Day we thank God for our rescue from the hand of our enemies round about, as explained there 4:3. Afterwards the State of Israel served as a refuge for every persecuted Jew, and the existence of a Jewish state raised the standing of Israel among the nations, and helped save Jewish lives. And see there 4:5-7 on the establishment of reciting Hallel on Independence Day, because it is a day of salvation for Israel, in going out to freedom from foreign rule, and in rescue from our enemies.

sections.title_en: The Halakhic Standing of the Mitzva
sections.body_en:
As we have learned, the Sages said of the mitzva of settling the Land (Sifrei Re'eh 53, Tosefta Avoda Zara 5:2): "Dwelling in the Land of Israel is equal to all the mitzvot in the Torah." It is true that they said of several other mitzvot too that they are equal to all the mitzvot; but from a halakhic point of view the mitzva of settling the Land has precedence over all the other mitzvot, for it is the only one we were commanded to fulfil with self-sacrifice, in conquering the Land and guarding it from the hand of our enemies (above, halakha 4).5

In addition, it is the only one that overrides a rabbinic 'shevut' prohibition on Shabbat. 'Shevut' is the name of the prohibitions the Sages instituted as a fence for keeping Shabbat. And they upheld their words so firmly that they established that even if a clash arises between fulfilling a Torah mitzva and a 'shevut' prohibition, the 'shevut' enactment is kept and the fulfilment of the Torah mitzva is set aside, because if people transgress the fences they will end up in full desecration of Shabbat. Therefore, if in order to fulfil the mitzva of circumcision on Shabbat one needs to carry a knife in a place where carrying is rabbinically forbidden, the circumcision is postponed and the words of the Sages are not transgressed.

Moreover, to prevent concern of a prohibition on Shabbat, the Sages established that when Rosh Ha-shana falls on Shabbat the shofar is not blown, lest people come to carry the shofar four amot in the public domain and transgress a Torah prohibition. And when the first day of the festival of Sukkot falls on Shabbat (on which there is a Torah mitzva to take the lulav everywhere), the lulav is not taken, lest people come to carry the lulav four amot in the public domain and transgress a Torah prohibition. It follows that all Israel refrain from the Torah positive mitzvot of blowing the shofar and taking the lulav because of a rabbinic 'shevut' prohibition.

And only for the sake of the mitzva of settling the Land did the Sages set aside a 'shevut' prohibition. For if it became possible for a Jew to buy a house from a gentile on Shabbat, and there is concern that after Shabbat he will lose the opportunity, he may carry out the acquisition and ask the gentile to write a deed for him on Shabbat, and show the gentile where the money is placed so that he may take it, without concern that this will lead to full desecration of Shabbat through writing or carrying. And we are not speaking here of saving the whole Land, but of redeeming one house of four by four amot; to redeem it the Sages permitted transgressing prohibitions of their own making, which they did not permit for other mitzvot (OḤ 306:11).6

notes_en.en: Similarly they said in Nedarim 32a of the mitzva of circumcision; in Bava Batra 9a of the mitzva of tzedaka; in Shevu'ot 29a of the mitzva of tzitzit; in Menaḥot 43b of tefillin; in the Yerushalmi Nedarim 3:9 of the mitzva of Shabbat; and there, Pe'ah 1:1, of acts of kindness. And so they said in several places of the mitzva of Torah study. And see above 1, note 8, on what is common to the mitzvot that are equal to all the mitzvot. But as explained above, from a halakhic point of view the mitzva of settling the Land exceeds the other mitzvot, for it is the only one for whose fulfilment one must be ready for self-sacrifice. For even the three mitzvot of which they said "be killed and do not transgress" apply only if it has come to that, that he is placed before two options, to transgress one of the three grave transgressions or to be killed; then he must be killed and not transgress. And likewise at a time of a royal decree it is a mitzva to give up one's life for all the mitzvot. But from the outset one must try to keep away from a situation in which he will be compelled to transgress and will have to give up his life. Whereas to conquer the Land, one must be ready from the outset to go out to war and risk lives.

For other mitzvot they permitted only a 'shevut de-shevut', that is, a weaker prohibition, as explained in SA OḤ 307:5. And I mentioned in note 1 that the source of this is Bava Kamma 80b and Gittin 8b, and Tosafot there. And see Peninei Halakha Shabbat 9:11-12. The great later authorities of Israel pointed to this law when they wanted to explain the superiority of the mitzva of settling the Land over the other mitzvot.

sections.title_en: A Disagreement Between Spouses
sections.body_en:
As a rule, when there is a disagreement between spouses about where to live, one side cannot compel the other to uproot from his place, because every uprooting to a strange place creates difficulties; therefore the one who wants to stay can argue that from his point of view the familiar place of residence is preferable, and his spouse cannot compel him to worsen his living conditions. But if they live in a town whose majority are gentiles, one of the spouses can compel the other to move to a place whose majority are Jews (and these laws are detailed in SA EH siman 75).

But all this is said when two places outside the Land or two places in the Land are under consideration. But when one side wants to go up to the Land, the law is with him. And it makes no difference whether it is the man or the woman: the one who refuses must set aside his view and go up to the Land. And even if outside the Land they live in a place whose majority are Jews, and in the Land of Israel they will be forced to live in a place whose majority are gentiles, the mitzva of settling the Land takes precedence.

And if, despite the halakha, the side that wants to remain in exile refuses to compromise and go up, and matters come to divorce, since the blame for the divorce lies on the one who refuses to go up, the Sages established that he loses the whole ketuba. That is, if the husband is the one who refuses to go up, he must pay the whole ketuba. And if the wife refuses to go up, she loses her whole ketuba (SA EH 75:4).

Once again we have learned of the greatness of the mitzva: everywhere the Torah's guidance is to strive to preserve shalom bayit, but when shalom bayit clashes with the mitzva of settling the Land, the mitzva of settling the Land takes precedence.

sections.title_en: Honouring Parents and Settling the Land
sections.body_en:
Question: When a son or daughter wants to go up to the Land of Israel and their parents firmly oppose it, is it proper, because of the mitzva of honouring parents, to listen to them and remain in the Diaspora, or does the mitzva of settling the Land take precedence and they must go up to the Land?

Answer: A basic condition of the mitzva of honouring parents is that honouring parents must not contradict any of the mitzvot of the Torah, not even a rabbinic mitzva. And if his parents told him to transgress something of the Torah, or demanded that he not fulfil one of the mitzvot of the Torah, he may not listen to them, because they too are commanded in the honour of the Omnipresent and in keeping the Torah (SA YD 240:15).

If so, since there is a mitzva to live in the Land, the son should not listen to his parents, and he must go up to the Land even against their will. All the more so with the mitzva of settling the Land, of which the Sages said (Sifrei Re'eh 53) that it is equal to all the mitzvot (responsa Maharam of Rothenburg 79; the Mabit 139; see Pitḥei Teshuva EH 75:6; and Yeḥaveh Da'at 3:69). And of course he should try to appease them with words.

And likewise one who wants to settle in a settlement in Yehuda and Shomron, so that the Land will be in our hands and not in the hand of another nation, and his parents worry and demand that he not settle in the place he has chosen: since there is a mitzva in settling, he need not listen to his parents. And of course he should try to appease them with words. It is worth adding that a comprehensive study found that life expectancy in the settlements of Yehuda and Shomron, in all age ranges, is higher than in the other parts of the country.

sections.title_en: Leaving the Land for an Important Need or a Trip
sections.body_en:
A central question in the laws of settling the Land is what the precise definition of the mitzva is. Is its essence that one's permanent place of residence be in the Land, but there is no obligation for a Jew to be in the Land at every single hour? Or is the essence of the mitzva that a person always live in the Land, and at every single moment there is a mitzva that he stay in the Land? On this halakhic definition depends the question whether one may leave the Land for a short trip abroad.

On the basis of the Talmud (Avoda Zara 13a), the Rambam ruled (Laws of Kings 5:9) that it is forbidden ever to leave the Land of Israel for outside the Land. But for three things they permitted leaving: Torah study, marriage and commerce, on condition that when he finishes his affairs he returns to the Land; but to dwell outside the Land permanently is forbidden. And if there is a severe famine in the Land, one may leave for outside the Land for a long time. And even in a situation of severe famine, it is a measure of piety to remain in the Land, as God commanded Yitzḥak our forefather at the time there was a famine: "Dwell in the land" (Bereshit 26:2). And public figures must be more careful about this, because by their going down they weaken the public; and therefore Elimelekh, who went down to Mo'av at a time of famine, was punished and died together with his two sons (Rut 1; Bava Batra 91a).

It follows, then, that there are two levels in the mitzva of dwelling in the Land. The first is establishing one's place of residence, and only when there is a severe famine, to the point that one can barely survive in the Land, is it permitted to establish one's home outside the Land. But otherwise, it is a mitzva for a Jew to establish his home in the Land of Israel. By the kindness of God, in recent generations, even in years of crisis the situation in the Land is reasonable; therefore it is a mitzva for every Jew to establish his home in the Land, and it is forbidden to go down from the Land in order to settle elsewhere.

The second level is staying in the Land, which should not be cancelled for nothing. But one may leave for outside the Land for a limited time for the sake of commerce and livelihood. And likewise one who has not succeeded in finding a wife in the Land may go abroad to find a spouse and afterwards go up to the Land. And likewise one who wants to learn from a particular rabbi who lives outside the Land may go out and learn from him, on condition that he plans to return afterwards. Indeed in recent times the great majority of Torah scholars live in the Land, and therefore there is almost no reason to go abroad to learn Torah there. But it is very common that rabbis and educators from the Land are asked to go abroad to teach Torah there and to educate towards aliya to the Land, and this is permitted and a mitzva. One may also leave the Land for medical treatment. And likewise one may leave for a short period for the sake of honouring parents.

But for a trip, according to many it is forbidden to go abroad, for we have learned that only for a great need, such as Torah study, livelihood and marriage, did they permit it, and not for a trip (Yeḥaveh Da'at 5:57; Aseh Lekha Rav 8:49).

However, it seems that if the departure is for a short time, for example for a period of less than a month, and the one leaving buys himself a 'return ticket', there is no prohibition in it. For this departure is utterly different from the departure discussed in the Talmud, in the Rambam and in the poskim. In those days one who went abroad would go for a long time, for the journey itself lasted months; consequently one who had already gone abroad would go for a prolonged stay, and there was even a certain concern that he would not return. And likewise the reasons for which the Sages permitted leaving the Land require a departure for a prolonged time, of a year and even more. For one who went out to marry had to find a bride, become engaged to her and marry. And likewise one who went out to learn Torah had to sit before his teacher many months, and usually several years. Even one who wanted to go on a trip abroad in those days would be away for a long time, many months, with the time of return uncertain. So all the permission the Sages dealt with concerns departure for a prolonged time, but they did not speak of departure for a short time, for there is no obligation to be in the Land of Israel at every single moment. Therefore there is no prohibition in going on a short trip. And especially when a mitzva aim is added to the trip, such as meeting Jews in the Diaspora and connecting them to Judaism and to the Land, or to grow wiser by seeing different people and sights.

Indeed at every single moment that a Jew is in the Land of Israel he fulfils a mitzva. And the principal virtue of the mitzvot is when they are fulfilled in the Land. It follows that one who leaves the Land, although he does not transgress a prohibition, loses during the time of his stay abroad a significant part of the virtue of the mitzvot and their reward; and therefore it is good always to be in the Land.7

In the days of the Second Temple, when the Sages decreed impurity upon the land of the nations, that is, upon the territories outside the border of the Jewish settlement of those who came up from Bavel, kohanim were forbidden to go outside the border of those who came up from Bavel even for one moment, and only for the sake of livelihood, marrying a wife or learning Torah were they permitted to leave (Avoda Zara 13a). But today, when purity is not practised, kohanim may go outside the border of those who came up from Bavel, like any Israelite.8

notes_en.en:
Among those who are stringent not to go on a trip abroad: Yeḥaveh Da'at 5:57; Aseh Lekha Rav 8:49; and so it is implied from the words of our master the Rav in Mishpat Kohen 147; and so it is implied from Rav Goren in 'Be-mishnat Ha-medina' p. 31, in a question about Eilat. And so it is brought in the book 'Eretz Tziltzal Kenafayim' in the name of Rav Lior and Rav Zalman Neḥemya Goldberg. And Rav Ariel inclines this way in Ohala Shel Torah 2:9. Among the lenient: Rav Yisraeli in Eretz Ḥemda, book 1, 1:10, who was lenient to leave on condition of returning for any need, even an optional one; but with no need at all it is forbidden. And so wrote the Shevet Ha-levi 5:173. And so wrote Rav Shlomo Dichovsky in Teḥumin 20. And so it seems to me in my humble opinion, according to the reasoning I wrote above. It further seems that if the prohibition on leaving were even for a short while, it would be forbidden to leave the borders of the Land even for a distance of a hundred metres in order to buy vegetables cheaply, and we have not found in the words of the Sages any discussion defining such a prohibition and the borders of the Land for this law. And I wrote "for example thirty days" because we learn in the words of the Sages that less than thirty days is a temporary time; therefore those who live in a city for thirty days are already considered residents of the city (Bava Batra 8a), and one who lives in an inn for less than thirty days is exempt from mezuza (SA YD 286:22). Indeed it is proper to conduct oneself so as not to go on a trip of more than thirty days, but this should not be established as a complete obligation.
Indeed even according to the lenient there is a mitzva to remain every moment in the Land of Israel, for the principal fulfilment of the mitzvot is in the Land, as the Sages said in Sifrei Ekev 37, and Rashi Devarim 11:18, and Ramban Vayikra 18:25, and as brought above 1:3. And our teacher and master the Ratziya transmitted in the name of the 'Ḥafetz Ḥayim' that by his calculation a mitzva in the Land of Israel is reckoned twenty times a mitzva outside the Land. However, one can say that the essence of the matter depends on the place of residence, as the language of the Sages, "whoever dwells in the Land of Israel is like one who has a God"; and one can say that the intention of 'dwells' is a permanent place of residence. And then one who goes abroad for positive purposes, even when he is abroad, is in the category of dwelling in the Land of Israel, for his whole world and aims are bound up with the Land of Israel; and therefore the virtue of his fulfilment of mitzvot abroad, too, is close to the virtue of their fulfilment in the Land of Israel. But if he goes on an ordinary trip, he indeed loses more of the virtue of the Land of Israel. It should be noted that sometimes there is a more serious problem with trips abroad: people go to places where it is hard to keep a Jewish way of life, and they distance themselves from fulfilling the mitzvot, and the damage may be very serious.
It seems that there is no loss of virtue in going on a trip from the border of those who came up from Egypt to the territories of the whole Land, such as to southern Sinai and the mountains of Edom in southern Jordan. However, regarding establishing a place of residence, since the places outside the border of those who came up from Egypt were not sanctified for the mitzvot, dwelling there does not have the virtue of dwelling in the places that were sanctified. And only when people settle there on the mission of the whole of Israel, for the sake of the mitzva of settling the Land, in order to expand the borders of the Land, will dwelling there be a great mitzva.

Since kohanim are forbidden to become impure through a dead body, after the Sages decreed impurity of the dead upon the land of the nations, that is, upon the places outside the border of those who came up from Bavel, kohanim were forbidden to go there. And some say that even today, when purity is not practised, kohanim may not leave the border of those who came up from Bavel, just as they may not become impure through a dead body even though they are already impure. And so wrote the Rambam (Laws of Mourning 3:14), SA (YD 372:1; 369:1); Shevut Ya'akov (2:98). But the Maharshal (YD 369) wrote that the prohibition of leaving the border of those who came up from Bavel applied only when the kohanim kept themselves in purity; but today, when everyone is impure through the dead, this law too is void. And so wrote there the Perisha, Baḥ, Shakh, Taz, and Rabbi Akiva Eiger in the name of the Mahariksh; Ḥokhmat Adam, Sha'ar Ha-simḥa 159:1. And since the basis of the impurity of the land of the nations is rabbinic, the halakha follows the lenient. All the more so there is no room to be stringent within the border of the State of Israel, for the basis of the prohibition is outside the border of settlement, and the whole territory of the State of Israel is today considered the border of settlement, as explained in Peninei Halakha Kashrut 12:17. (It is worth noting that from the definitions of the permission for kohanim to leave for a great need such as livelihood, marrying a wife and Torah study, we learned a permission for all Israel to go abroad for these needs (Rambam, Kings 5:9). Therefore some wanted to learn that just as kohanim were forbidden to leave without a great need even for one moment, so too Israelites should not leave even for a short trip without a great need. But in my humble opinion only the principle is learned from the kohanim, while the details of the prohibition differ: for kohanim it is forbidden to leave even for one moment because of the impurity of the land of the nations, whereas for Israelites the prohibition is only for a prolonged time, because of the mitzva of dwelling in the Land of Israel, which is permanent dwelling.)

sections.title_en: Love of the Land
sections.body_en:
From the Torah we have learned that one must appreciate the goodness of the Land and thank God for it, as it is said (Devarim 8:7-10): "For the Lord your God brings you into a good land, a land of brooks of water, of springs and depths that spring out in valleys and hills; a land of wheat and barley, and vines and fig trees and pomegranates; a land of olive oil and honey; a land in which you shall eat bread without scarceness, you shall not lack anything in it; a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills you may dig copper. And you shall eat and be satisfied, and you shall bless the Lord your God for the good land which He has given you." So the Torah educates us to love the Land of Israel, and out of this to thank God for it.

It is told in the Talmud (Ketubot 112a-b) that Rabbi Abba, when he would reach the border of the Land of Israel, would kiss its stones out of great love for the Land. And Rabbi Ḥiya bar Gamda would roll in its dust out of great love for it, to fulfil what is said (Tehillim 102:14-15): "You shall arise and have mercy upon Tziyon, for it is time to be gracious to her, for the appointed time has come. For Your servants take pleasure in her stones, and cherish her dust." And so wrote the Rambam (Laws of Kings 5:10): "The greatest of the Sages would kiss the borders of the Land of Israel, kiss its stones and roll in its dust, and so it says: For Your servants take pleasure in her stones, and cherish her dust." Seemingly one should ask: why did the Rambam write these practices in his book of halakha? Their place would seem to be in books of mussar and not in books of halakha. But we learn a great thing from this halakha: one must love the Land of Israel.

And so we find that throughout the exile the great ones of Israel sang songs of longing and yearning for the Land of Israel, such as Rabbi Yehuda Ha-levi in his poem "Tziyon, will you not ask": "Tziyon, will you not ask after the welfare of your captives, who seek your welfare and are the remnant of your flocks? From west and east, from north and south, take greetings, far and near, from all your sides; and the greeting of a captive of desire, who sheds his tears like the dew of Ḥermon and longs for them to fall upon your mountains. To weep for your affliction I am a jackal, and when I dream of the return of your captivity, I am a harp for your songs… Would that I could wander in the places where God was revealed to your seers and your messengers. Who will make me wings, that I may wander far, and carry the pieces of my heart among your broken mountains? I will fall on my face upon your land, and greatly cherish your stones and be gracious to your dust… It would be sweet to my soul to walk naked and barefoot over the desolate ruins that were your sanctuaries. Happy is he who waits and arrives and sees your light rise, and your dawns break forth upon him; to see the good of your chosen ones, and to exult in your joy when you return to the days of your youth." And in another poem: "Beautiful of view, joy of the world, city of a great King, for you my soul yearns from the ends of the west. My compassion is stirred when I remember of old your glory that went into exile and your dwelling that was destroyed. Who will set me upon the wings of eagles, until I water your dust with my tears and they mingle? Shall I not cherish your stones and kiss them, and the taste of your clods be sweeter in my mouth than honey?"

sections.title_en: The Mitzva to Praise the Land and the Prohibition of Speaking Ill of It
sections.body_en:
As we have learned (above 1:5), the root of the sin of the spies was that they did not love the Land, as it is said (Tehillim 106:24): "And they despised the desirable land, they did not believe His word." Out of this they spoke ill of it, as it is said (Bamidbar 13:32): "And they brought up an evil report of the land which they had spied out to the children of Israel, saying: The land through which we passed to spy it out is a land that devours its inhabitants."

Come and see the virtue of the Land of Israel: the prohibition of lashon ha-ra applies only to people, so as not to cause them pain; therefore there is no prohibition of speaking lashon ha-ra about trees and stones, which feel no pain. But about the Land of Israel it is forbidden to speak lashon ha-ra, because one who speaks ill of it denies the Torah, which praised the Land, and holds back the revelation of God's name in the world, which is revealed only through the Land of Israel, the Holy Land. Therefore the punishment of one who spreads an evil report about the Land is especially severe: even the generation of knowledge, who received the Torah at Sinai, were not protected by their merit; since they listened to lashon ha-ra about it and despised it, death was decreed upon them, and Israel's entry into the Land was delayed forty years.

And so it is told in the Talmud (Ketubot 112a) of the great Amoraim, who would strive that no bad name should go out about the Land of Israel. Rabbi Ḥanina, when he walked in the Land of Israel and saw an obstacle on the road, would repair it. And Rashi explained that he would level and repair the obstacles of the city out of love for the Land, which was dear to him; he would always go around to repair it so that no bad name would go out about its roads. And Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi were careful to seat their students in the most pleasant place: in the morning, when it was a little cold, they seated them in the sun, and at midday, when it became hot, they seated them in the shade, so that they would not, heaven forbid, complain about living in the Land and its climate.

We must repair the sin of the spies, speak in praise of the Land and thank God for the good gift He bequeathed to our forefathers and to us. And especially in our generation, when by the kindness of God millions of Jews have merited to go up to the Land, establish families in it and settle it, which many generations of righteous and holy ones before us did not merit. And therefore a double obligation is placed upon us: to be careful to speak in praise of the Land of Israel, to love its landscapes, to adorn it with trees and flowers, to clean it of litter, to repair its roads, to build pleasant and beautiful houses in it. And always to repeat the words of Yehoshua and Kalev, who stood against all the slanderers and said: "The land is exceedingly good" (Bamidbar 14:7). And by this we will repair the sin of the spies, and out of this more Jews will go up to the Land and fewer will leave, and we will merit to fulfil the great mitzva of 'settling the Land'.

Our master Rav Kook wrote (Igrot Ha-Re'aya, letter 96): "The foundation of the exile and the lowliness that continues in the world comes only from the fact that the Land of Israel is not made known, its value and its wisdom, and the sin of the spies, who spread an evil report about the Land, is not repaired by the corresponding repentance: to tell and proclaim in the whole world its glory and splendour, its holiness and its honour. And would that we merit, after all the exaltations on our part, to express even one part in ten thousand of the delight of the desirable land, of the splendour of the light of its Torah, of the elevation of the light of its wisdom, and of the holy spirit that is raised up within it."

sections.title_en: Settling the Land by Planting Trees and Developing the Economy
sections.body_en:
We have already learned (in halakha 1) that the mitzva of settling the Land is not only to conquer the Land so that it will be under the rule of Israel; rather, the mitzva is to settle in the Land throughout its length and breadth, so that it does not remain desolate. As the Ramban wrote: "that we should not leave it in the hand of others among the nations or to desolation, and this is what is said: And you shall take possession of the land and dwell in it."

And so the 'Ḥatam Sofer' wrote (in his novellae to tractate Sukka, daf 36) that working the land in the Land of Israel in order to bring forth its holy fruits involves the mitzva of settling the Land, and about this the Torah commanded "and you shall gather in your grain" (Devarim 11:14). And so Bo'az, who was the greatest of the generation, would himself winnow the threshing floor of barley all night, and was not concerned that this was neglect of Torah. And just as a person would not say, I will not put on tefillin because I am occupied with Torah, so he should not say, I will not gather my grain because of neglect of Torah. He further added that it is possible that all the labours and crafts that help settle the Land are included in the mitzva.

And in this the Land of Israel is unique: outside the Land there is no mitzva for a Jew to plant trees and develop the economy beyond the needs of his livelihood. But in the Land of Israel, even one whose livelihood is secure has a mitzva to plant fruit trees and engage in developing the economy. For the Land of Israel is the Holy Land; that is, even in its physicality there is holiness, and everyone who helps its building, development and flourishing is a partner in building holiness.

The Sages said (Vayikra Rabba 25:3): "It is said (Devarim 13:5): After the Lord your God shall you walk. But is it possible for flesh and blood to walk after the Holy One, blessed be He? And it is also said (Devarim 13:5): And to Him shall you cleave. But is it possible for flesh and blood to cleave to the Shekhina? Rather, walk in His ways and cleave to His attributes. Just as the Holy One, blessed be He, at the beginning of the creation of the world occupied Himself first only with planting, as it is said (Bereshit 2:8): And the Lord God planted a garden in Eden, so you too, when you enter the Land, occupy yourselves first only with planting; this is what is said (Vayikra 19:23): And when you come into the land and plant." We thus learn that one who plants a tree in the Land of Israel cleaves to the attributes of the Holy One, blessed be He.

Planting trees has two advantages. The first: a long-term investment. Sometimes people tend at the beginning of their way to invest in passing things, and the Torah guides us to settle permanently in the Land, like those who plant trees, who plan their investment for the long term; and through this we become more rooted in the Land of Israel. The second: through the trees the Land brings forth its holy fruits, which we eat, and many mitzvot, such as shevi'it, terumot and ma'asrot, are fulfilled with them.

Rabbi Natan Shapira, a disciple of the holy Ari, asked: why, when our forefathers were in the wilderness, did they merit to eat the manna, which is miraculous and heavenly food, whereas when they entered the Holy Land the manna stopped falling? And he answered that the wilderness and outside the Land are impure places that are not capable of receiving holiness in their fruits, and it was necessary to bring down manna for them from heaven so that they would not become defiled by coarse foods, and so they could absorb the Torah. But in the Land of Israel, which is the Holy Land, holiness is revealed and clothes itself in the holy fruits, and therefore they did not need manna from heaven. His colleague Rabbi Moshe Zakut added to his words that, on the contrary, the holiness in the fruits of the Land of Israel exceeds the manna, for by eating them in holiness a repair and refinement is made for physical reality (the book 'Tuv Ha-aretz' by Rav Natan Shapira).

And so Rav Kook explained that the holiness of the Land of Israel is a holiness revealed through nature, whereas the Shekhina that went down with us into exile has the capacity to set holiness against nature, but this is a holiness that is not complete. And our aspiration is to reveal the complete holiness, in all areas of life, and this can be revealed only in the Land of Israel (Orot Ha-teḥiya 28). And this is the special virtue of the Torah of the Land of Israel, which reveals the word of God in the world, in all areas of life, and through this complete faith is revealed in a complete life (as explained above 1:1-2).

sections.title_en: Gradual Fulfilment of the Mitzva of Settling the Land to Its Borders
sections.body_en:
The mitzva of settling the Land applies in principle to all the borders of the Land of Israel that the Holy One, blessed be He, promised to Avraham our forefather, as it is said (Bereshit 15:18): "On that day the Lord made a covenant with Avram, saying: To your seed I have given this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Perat." And so it is said (Shemot 23:31): "And I will set your border from the Sea of Reeds to the sea of the Philistines, and from the wilderness to the River, for I will deliver the inhabitants of the land into your hand, and you shall drive them out before you." And as we were commanded (Devarim 1:7-8): "Turn and take your journey, and go to the hill country of the Emori and to all the places near it, in the Arava, in the hill country and in the lowland, and in the Negev and by the seashore, the land of the Kena'ani, and the Levanon, as far as the great river, the river Perat. Behold, I have set the land before you; go in and possess the land which the Lord swore to your fathers, to Avraham, to Yitzḥak and to Ya'akov, to give to them and to their seed after them." And so it is said (Devarim 11:24): "Every place on which the sole of your foot shall tread shall be yours; from the wilderness and the Levanon, from the river, the river Perat, to the western sea shall be your border." And so it is said (Yehoshua 1:3-4): "Every place on which the sole of your foot shall tread I have given to you, as I spoke to Moshe. From the wilderness and this Levanon to the great river, the river Perat, all the land of the Ḥittim, and to the great sea toward the going down of the sun, shall be your border."

In practice, however, the mitzva of settling the Land must be fulfilled gradually, according to the ability of the people of Israel. Therefore the divine guidance was to conquer first the western bank of the Jordan according to the borders in parashat Mas'ei, which are the more sanctified territories of the Land, and only after they had settled all the territories in their hand would they gradually expand to the eastern bank of the Jordan and all the territories of the Land of Israel (Ramban Bamidbar 21:21). Therefore at first Moshe our teacher did not intend to conquer the land of Siḥon and Og, and only after Siḥon and Og did not accept Israel's offer of peace and went out against them to war did the people of Israel conquer their land. And after the tribes of Reuven and Gad asked to take their inheritance on the eastern bank of the Jordan, Moshe our teacher agreed to their request, on condition that they too take part in the conquest of the more sanctified part, which is on the western bank of the Jordan (and see above 2:1).9

Rabbi Shimon ben Tzemaḥ wrote (Tashbetz 3:200) that in terms of holiness and the resting of the Shekhina, the virtue of the western bank of the Jordan is higher, and therefore Moshe our teacher longed to cross the Jordan. And likewise what the Sages said (Ketubot 111a), "Whoever is buried in the Land of Israel is as though buried under the altar", and through this his sins are atoned, was said of the western bank of the Jordan. And likewise what they said (Yevamot 64a), that by the merit of the Land of Israel a couple who have not merited children for ten years can be remembered, was said of the western bank of the Jordan. And so the Sages said (Bamidbar Rabba 7:8): "The land of Kena'an is more sanctified than the other side of the Jordan; the land of Kena'an is fit for the house of the Shekhina, and the other side of the Jordan is not fit for the house of the Shekhina." That is, one cannot establish the Mishkan or the Temple on the eastern bank of the Jordan for a permanent time. But in terms of the mitzva of settling the Land, there is no difference between the eastern bank of the Jordan and the western bank of the Jordan; therefore a husband or wife can compel their spouse to go up from outside the Land to the eastern bank of the Jordan. But they could not compel moving from the eastern bank of the Jordan to the western bank of the Jordan, because regarding the mitzvot dependent on the Land, the eastern bank of the Jordan is equal to the western.10

Within the western bank of the Jordan too there is a gradation, and Yehuda and Shomron are the places that must be settled first, for they are the most sanctified: the forefathers walked in them, the prophecies to the forefathers and the prophets were revealed in them, they were the centre of Jewish life in the Land, and in them stood the Mishkan of Shilo and the Temple in Jerusalem; and therefore the olim from Bavel strove to take hold of them first. And from there the mitzva expands gradually to all the borders explained in parashat Mas'ei, and afterwards to fill out the border of the Land of Israel.11

Rav Avraham Azulai (the great-grandfather of the Ḥida) wrote in the book 'Ḥesed Le-Avraham' (Ma'ayan 3, Nahar 7): "And just as the Shekhina is not in completeness as long as the place of the Temple is not complete on its foundation, so too the Shekhina is not in completeness as long as the Land of Israel is not complete in all its borders, which is from the brook of Egypt to the great river, the river Perat, and Israel dwell each one in the portion due to him according to the portion of his true border."

notes_en.en:
From the episode of the children of Reuven and Gad, who wanted to inherit on the eastern bank of the Jordan (Bamidbar 32), it emerges clearly that the first aim was that everyone would first enter the western part, and from the sanctified core they would afterwards spread out and inherit the eastern side too. Also from the longing of Moshe our teacher to enter the Land it is implied that as long as he had not entered the western side of the Jordan, he had not yet entered the core of the Land. Similarly we have learned that the Torah commanded that after we merit to expand our border we should establish three more cities of refuge, as it is said (Devarim 19:8-9): "And if the Lord your God enlarges your border, as He swore to your fathers, and gives you all the land which He promised to give to your fathers… then you shall add three more cities for yourself, besides these three."
And one should also ask: we learned in Bamidbar 34, in the passage in which the borders of the Land are mentioned in detail, that the northern border begins in the west at Hor Ha-har, and about the location of Hor Ha-har we learned in halakha 16 four opinions. And there in the verses the border of the Land does not extend to the river Perat; rather, at some point it begins to descend southward until it reaches the Kinneret. And one should ask why the border was not marked up to the river Perat. And the Malbim explained that the Torah said in this passage "for you" several times, until it concluded "this shall be the land for you", "to hint that it is only for the time being, for the border will expand each time, as it was in the days of David and Shlomo and in the days of Herod, when their kingdom spread to the river Perat, and all the more so in the future to come." So because we were still relatively few, we were commanded to conquer what was in our power on the western side. As it is said (Shemot 23:30): "Little by little I will drive them out from before you, until you have increased and inherit the land." We learn from this that when it is in our power to settle part of the Land, the western side should be preferred first. And so too the individuals who went up to the Land during two thousand years of exile conducted themselves, trying to take hold on the western side, in Jerusalem, Ḥevron, Shekhem, Aza, Tzfat, Teveria and the like, cities that are on the western side of the Jordan.

As we have learned, regarding the mitzvot the status of the eastern bank of the Jordan is like the status of the western bank of the Jordan; and so they said in Mishna Shevi'it 9:2, "Three lands for removal": Yehuda, the other side of the Jordan and the Galil. And in Sanhedrin 11b: "For three lands the year is intercalated: Yehuda, the other side of the Jordan and the Galil." And they disagreed regarding bikkurim: according to the Tanna Kamma in Mishna Bikkurim 1:10, bikkurim are brought from fruits on the other side of the Jordan, for this is included in 'your land'. And according to R. Yosei they are not brought, for although it is the Land of Israel, nevertheless it is not included under the name "a land flowing with milk and honey". And so too the view of R. Shimon is that bikkurim are not brought from the other side of the Jordan, for one must bring from the land "which You have given me", excluding the other side of the Jordan, which you took for yourself. And the halakha follows the Tanna Kamma, that bikkurim are brought from the other side of the Jordan. Moreover, we have learned that R. Yoḥanan wondered how it was possible that those who came up from Bavel to the Land of Israel reached an anger that led to murder, and Ulla answered him that this was before they crossed the Jordan (Nedarim 22a). And in my humble opinion, after Israel settle the other side of the Jordan properly, the holiness of the Land and its tranquillity will spread there too.
Regarding the Golan, there is reason to say that it is included in the Galil, and its holiness is like the western bank of the Jordan, for the eastern bank of the Jordan extends southward from the Kinneret, but the Golan is included in the Galil.

When there was a famine in the days of Yitzḥak our forefather, he wanted to go down to Egypt like his father; "and the Lord appeared to him and said: Do not go down to Egypt; dwell in the land of which I shall tell you. Sojourn in this land…" (Bereshit 26:2-3). And it is said (ibid. 12): "And Yitzḥak sowed in that land, and found in that year a hundredfold…" Rashi explained: "In that land: even though it is not as important as the Land of Israel itself, as the land of the seven nations." We find, then, that the southern lowland is not as important as Yehuda, Shomron and the Galil. And therefore when Yitzḥak went down to live in it, this was a kind of compromise.

sections.title_en: The Southern Borders: The Brook and the River of Egypt
sections.body_en:
The south-western border of the whole Land of Israel is the 'river of Egypt', as it is said (Bereshit 15:18): "To your seed I have given this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Perat." It is agreed that the river of Egypt is the eastern branch of the Nile, which is in the area of today's Suez Canal. Regarding the southern border it is said (Shemot 23:31): "And I will set your border from the Sea of Reeds to the sea of the Philistines", implying that the whole Sinai peninsula is within the border of Israel, for the Sea of Reeds surrounds it, and it was set as the southern border.12

But the command to those who came up from Egypt under the leadership of Yehoshua bin Nun was to conquer a border line that begins south of the Dead Sea and runs to the 'brook of Egypt', as explained in parashat Mas'ei (Bamidbar 34:5); and only after they had properly settled the core of the Land would they spread out to all the borders of the Land. The poskim disagreed about the southern border that those who came up from Egypt were commanded to conquer, and the disagreement depends on the identification of the places mentioned in parashat Mas'ei from south of the Dead Sea to the brook of Egypt. Some say that the border curves slightly south of the Dead Sea and includes the town of Yeruḥam and Sde Boker, and then curves north again to the brook of Egypt. And some say that it extends further south to Ein Yahav in the Arava and Mitzpe Ramon in the Negev, and from there runs to the brook of Egypt. And some hold that it goes south to Eilat and from there runs to the brook of Egypt.

They further disagreed about what the 'brook of Egypt' is. According to most of the Rishonim and some Aḥaronim, the 'brook of Egypt' is identical with the 'river of Egypt', which is the eastern branch of the Nile (Targum Yonatan and Yerushalmi, Rashi, Rambam, Tosafot, Roke'aḥ, Radak, Rash Sirillo, Gra). And according to many of the Aḥaronim, following some of the Rishonim, the 'brook of Egypt' is Wadi el-Arish (Rasag, Kaftor Va-feraḥ, Radbaz).

The significance of the discussion of how far the border of those who came up from Egypt extends is for two matters: first, the obligation of settling the Land: whether it is at a high order of priority, like the borders of parashat Mas'ei, or at a low one, like the rest of the borders of the promised Land. Second, the obligation of the mitzvot dependent on the Land as long as there is no Israeli sovereignty there. However, a place that is under Israeli sovereignty and is within the borders of the whole Land is in any case obligated in the mitzvot dependent on the Land, like the border of those who came up from Bavel.13

notes_en.en: The border of the whole Land: According to all opinions the southern border of the whole Land extends at least to Eilat, as it is said (Shemot 23:31): "And I will set your border from the Sea of Reeds to the sea of the Philistines." Simply understood, the intention is the whole Sinai peninsula, for this is the natural border, and it is the border of the Sea of Reeds mentioned in the Torah. And this is the view of: Rashi; Otzar Neḥmad on the Kuzari 2:14; Iggeret Orḥot Olam chapter 8. And likewise of Rav Yisrael Ariel shlit"a (Otzar Eretz Yisrael vol. 5, 30). However, according to my teacher Rav Ḥayim Steiner shlit"a (Tova Ha-aretz, Sha'ar Darom 1, p. 19), the Rambam's view is that the brook of Egypt and the river of Egypt are the Nile, with the southern line running from Eilat to the point parallel to it at latitude 29.5 on the Nile (so that the Rambam, who lived in old Cairo, on the east of the Nile, lived within the territory of the Land of Israel, as the Mahariksh wrote, Erekh Leḥem, Even Ha-ezer 128), and the southern part of the Sinai peninsula is not included in the Land of Israel. For it is implied from the Rambam that the border line runs from Eilat to the Nile: in Laws of Sanctification of the Month 18:16 he wrote that it is latitude thirty, and there 11:17 it is implied that it is at latitude twenty-nine; so the line is in between, and that is where Eilat is. Moreover, one can say that the deserts were not set within the border of the Land because they are not a place of settlement, and the whole southern part of Sinai is a mountainous desert. But this is difficult to say, since the northern part of Sinai too is desert, and the natural border in the south is the sea surrounding the Sinai peninsula.

The southern border of parashat Mas'ei: Bamidbar 34:3-5: "Then your southern side shall be from the wilderness of Tzin alongside Edom, and your southern border shall be from the end of the Dead Sea eastward. And your border shall turn from the south to the ascent of Akrabim, and pass on to Tzin, and its goings out shall be south of Kadesh Barne'a, and it shall go out to Ḥatzar Addar and pass on to Atzmon. And the border shall turn from Atzmon to the brook of Egypt, and its goings out shall be at the sea." As a rule, the borders of the Land must be natural borders: a river or a seasonal stream or the edge of a desert or a sea. There are three opinions identifying the course of the southern border in parashat Mas'ei, beginning south of the Dead Sea. a) 'Tevu'ot Ha-aretz': it begins south of the Dead Sea towards Naḥal Tzin by way of Ne'ot Ha-kikar, and from there to Wadi el-Arish. Under this border Yeruḥam and Sde Boker are inside the border and Mitzpe Ramon is south of it. b) 'Admat Kodesh': the border goes south from the Dead Sea to Ein Yahav and continues to the Ramon crater and from there to Wadi el-Arish. Mitzpe Ramon is inside this border. c) Some say that the southern border extends to Eilat and from there to the brook of Egypt (Rav Tykocinski, following Rasag, in the book Eretz Yisrael 26:2; Rav Eliyahu in Ma'amar Mordekhai 2:9, 23; Rav Steiner on the Rambam's view. And some are precise according to the Rambam that it is about 60 km north of Eilat, which is latitude 30).
The brook of Egypt is the south-western border of the Land of Israel in parashat Mas'ei, and they disagreed about its location:
a) Those who hold that the brook of Egypt is Wadi el-Arish are: Kaftor Va-feraḥ chapter 11, following Rasag; Radbaz vol. 4, 30. b) Those who hold that it is the eastern branch of the Nile delta are: Rashi (Shemot 10:19), the Kuzari (2:4; 4:3), Tosafot Yom Tov (Ta'anit 1:3, 2). And so it is implied that the brook of Egypt is the Nile from Targum Yonatan Bereshit 15 and Bamidbar 34:5, Targum Yerushalmi Bamidbar 34:5; Tosafot Arakhin 15a, 'ke-shem'; R. Eliyahu Mizraḥi Bamidbar 34:5; Radak Yehoshua 13:3; R. Shlomo Sirillo Shevi'it 6:1; Gra Yehoshua 15:10. According to all opinions the Gaza region and the Yamit region are included in the borders of the Land of Israel, not only in the borders of the promise but even in the borders of the conquest of the Land in the days of Yehoshua, and they were in the inheritance of Yehuda, as it is said (Yehoshua 15:47): "Aza, its towns and its villages, to the brook of Egypt and the great sea and its border."
Some say that the discussions about the border of parashat Mas'ei determine the status of the places regarding the obligation of terumot, ma'asrot and shevi'it in our time. But in practice it seems that after Israeli sovereignty was applied to all these territories up to Eilat, this disagreement has no halakhic significance, for Israeli sovereignty and Jewish settlement continue the border of the holiness of those who came up from Bavel to every place, as I wrote in Peninei Halakha Shevi'it Ve-yovel 5:8, note 8; and more at length in Peninei Halakha Kashrut 12:17, notes 20-21. One can further say that even according to those who hold that the southern part of the Sinai peninsula is not included in the borders of the Land, after we conquered the whole Sinai peninsula in the Six-Day War, which was a war of mitzva for the defence of the people and the Land, all would agree that throughout the period of the conquest the Sinai peninsula was considered the Land of Israel for all the mitzvot; for they said in Sifrei Devarim 11: "From the wilderness: and the wilderness is not your border; if you have conquered it, the wilderness too is your border, etc." And so it is implied from the Ramban there. And so wrote the Mishpat Kohen, that when there is no king, the whole nation is in place of the king. And see Tzitz Eliezer vol. 10, siman 1.
And although I wrote that the border of those who came up from Egypt is considered of a higher order of priority for the mitzva of settling the Land, one should not say that as long as we have not settled the whole border of those who came up from Egypt, one should not settle territories of the Land of Israel outside the border of those who came up from Egypt; according to political considerations it may be possible to give precedence to settling places outside the border of those who came up from Egypt over territories within the border of those who came up from Egypt whose settlement is difficult for various reasons (and see Peninei Halakha Kashrut 12:3, on the deficiency in the conquest of Syria, which was considered an individual's conquest, because it was not conquered for the sake of settlement. And see there 12, note 20, regarding Sinai, that whatever was conquered within the framework of a war of mitzva is sanctified regarding the mitzvot dependent on the Land, even when there are territories within the border of those who came up from Bavel and from Egypt that are not in our hands).
