sections.title_en: The Northern Borders: Hor Ha-har
sections.body_en:
The northern border in parashat Mas'ei begins in the west, from the sea, at a place near Hor Ha-har, as it is said (Bamidbar 34:7): "And this shall be your northern border: from the great sea you shall mark out for yourselves Hor Ha-har." The question is where Hor Ha-har is, and whether it is the northern border of the whole Land of Israel or only the northern border for those who came up from Egypt, who, after they grew strong, would conquer further, up to the river Perat.

There are five opinions identifying Hor Ha-har:
• According to Targum Yonatan and Targum Yerushalmi (Bamidbar 34:7) it is in the mountain range called 'Taurus Amanus', which are the Amanus Mountains in southern Turkey, north of latitude 36.
• According to 'Kaftor Va-feraḥ' (chapter 11) it is a mountain called 'Akra', today called 'Mount Kel', on the border between Turkey and Syria, at latitude 36.
• According to the Rambam the northern border is at latitude 35 (Laws of Sanctification of the Month 11:17), and it begins on the western side at a mountain near the town of 'Baniyas'.
• According to R. Shlomo Sirillo (Shevi'it 6:1) and 'Tevu'ot Ha-aretz' (chapter 1), it is a mountain slightly south of Tripoli, today called 'Mount Batrun'.
• According to 'Admat Kodesh' (chapter 1) it is near Beirut, to its east, on a mountain today called 'Ḥamana'.

Apparently, according to the fourth and fifth opinions, the place of Hor Ha-har is the border that those who came up from Egypt were commanded to conquer and divide among the tribes. But it is difficult to say that in their view it is the border of the whole Land, for according to their view one cannot draw a natural border between the river Perat and Hor Ha-har. And therefore it is reasonable that in their view the border of the whole Land is as the first or second opinion.

Conversely, according to the first opinion, Hor Ha-har is indeed the border of the whole Land, and one can draw from it a natural border of about 180 km to the river Perat. But what Israel were commanded to conquer in parashat Mas'ei, it is reasonable, includes only the Lebanon mountains. So there is no great disagreement regarding the northern border, because the narrowing opinions deal with the border of parashat Mas'ei, and the broadening opinion deals with the border of the whole Land. And it seems that the border of parashat Mas'ei is as the fifth opinion, and the border of the whole Land as the first opinion.14

notes_en.en:
The northern border of parashat Mas'ei: All the opinions identifying Hor Ha-har as the northern border of those who came up from Egypt face a difficulty: how could the tribe of Asher have been given so large an inheritance? For even according to the fifth opinion, it turns out that it was given a larger territory than the other tribes, for it included most of the Galil and nearly half the Lebanon mountains up to Beirut, a very large and fertile territory. All the more so is the fourth opinion difficult, which includes all the Lebanon mountains up to Tripoli. And all the more so the opinions that go further north. And one can explain that at first all twelve tribes were meant to inherit on the western bank of the Jordan up to Levo Ḥamat, which is mentioned as the northern border near Hor Ha-har, as it is said of the spies whom Moshe sent, that they spied out the Land up to Levo Ḥamat (Bamidbar 13:21). And even after Reuven, Gad and half of Menashe inherited on the eastern bank of the Jordan, the northern border of the Land still remained at Hor Ha-har and Levo Ḥamat, as a border to aspire to. Indeed, the division of the Land among the tribes in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun was only up to Tzidon, to which the inheritance of the tribe of Asher extended. And what is north of the inheritance of Asher up to Levo Ḥamat, and likewise the Lebanon mountains east of Tzidon, were meant for whoever would lack room, just as the children of Dan came to Leshem, which is near Kiryat Shmona. And the disagreement between the identifications is how far the Land was supposed to reach had the twelve tribes inherited on the western bank of the Jordan: whether to the area of Beirut, or the area of Tripoli, or to Baniyas in central Syria, and according to Kaftor Va-feraḥ to Mount Akra in southern Turkey. A certain support for the fourth opinion is that it is implied that all the Lebanon mountains are included in the Land of Israel (Yehoshua 13:5), and this opinion indeed includes all the Lebanon mountains, which extend to the area of Tripoli. And likewise the city of Geval, which is north of Beirut, is included in the borders of the Land of Israel (ibid.). On the other hand, we have not heard that the border of settlement to which those who came up from Egypt aspired to reach extends north of the Lebanon mountains.
A certain support for the fifth opinion is that in practice this is as far as Israel inherited, for we have learned that the mitzva is to set the cities of refuge at equal distances between them, and between the northernmost of them and the border of the Land (Makkot 9b). And since the northern city of refuge in the Galil is Kedesh (about 25 km north of the Kinneret), consequently the border of the Land must end near the area of Beirut. And then according to this reasoning, even if all twelve tribes had inherited on the western bank of the Jordan, they would have reached there, if they had inherited all the territories fully, without leaving Canaanites.
But the first and second opinions are very difficult: how could the border of Mas'ei be so far north, up to Turkey, and we have not found a great complaint against those who inherited the Land in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun for failing to conquer all these vast territories, but only that they did not conquer the Lebanon (Yehoshua 13:5; Shoftim 3:3)? And even if all the children of Reuven and Gad had inherited there, they would not have filled even half the territory, for it is much more fertile than the territory they actually received. Nor can this region be called 'the western bank of the Jordan', for the Jordan marks only about a third of the territory of this land (and so remarked Rav Yisraeli in 'Eretz Ḥemda' 1:4:5, and Rav Steiner in 'Tova Ha-aretz' p. 130). Therefore it is reasonable that the first opinion, which is the view of the Targumim, deals with the border of the whole Land, and they relied on the indication of Hor Ha-har without being precise. One can further explain that in their view the Torah hinted by the indication of Hor Ha-har at two places, the border of Mas'ei and the complete border. And the fact that the complete northern border is hinted at in parashat Mas'ei is meant to teach that one must spread out up to there. However, Kaftor Va-feraḥ is difficult, for he identified Mount Akra and the places near it with the places mentioned in parashat Mas'ei.
The northern border of the whole Land: The rule is that the borders of the Land are natural borders, and therefore the northern border must connect from Hor Ha-har to the river Perat in a natural way. According to the first and second opinions, this is a short border between the Mediterranean and the bend of the Perat, and it passes through fairly desert places, so that it hardly cuts through settled land. With great difficulty one could explain the Rambam's view this way too; but simply, latitude 35 cannot be accepted as the northern border, since its connection to the river Perat is not natural, because it would have to cut through the middle of the chain of the 'Ansariya Mountains', whose height is over 1,000 metres, and afterwards it runs diagonally within a great desert. And all the more so one cannot draw a natural border line from Hor Ha-har to the river Perat according to the fourth and fifth opinions. Therefore it is reasonable that in their view the northern border of the whole Land of Israel is according to the first or second opinion.
[Map of the northern border]

sections.title_en: The Eastern Border of the Whole Land
sections.body_en: The eastern border is not explained in the Torah; rather, it is said that the Land of Israel extends to the river Perat. The question is whether up to the northern side, near the core of the Land, or along its whole length up to the Persian Gulf. The reasoning for the northern side is that in the territory between the eastern bank of the Jordan and the end of the river Perat there is a vast desert, in which people were not accustomed to live, and perhaps it is the desert that was indicated as the border of the Land of Israel, as it is said (Shemot 23:31): "And I will set your border from the Sea of Reeds to the sea of the Philistines, and from the wilderness to the River." On the other hand, it is possible that the whole river Perat up to the Persian Gulf is the border of the Land, for otherwise we do not know where the border of the Land of Israel ends, and the border of the desert is south of there. In practice the Rishonim disagreed about this: some say that the river Perat marks the northern border of the Land, and some say that it marks the eastern border too.15

notes_en.en:
There are two opinions about the eastern border. a) In Otzar Neḥmad on the Kuzari he wrote that the river Perat is the eastern border up to the Persian Gulf, and so it is implied from the view of the great sage R. Moshe son of R. Ḥisdai the Frenchman that the river Perat is the eastern border, and the Ramban and Ritva (Gittin 7b) recorded his view. And so it is implied in I Divrei Ha-yamim 5:9, and Radak and Metzudot there. And so wrote Iggeret Orḥot Olam chapters 8 and 10. And so it is brought in the book of Rav Yisrael Ariel, part 2, 12:4. A great proof of this is that the Amora Rav, who lived in Sura in southern Bavel, asked his son to build him a house on the western side of the Perat, for there is the Land of Israel (Bereshit Rabba 16:3). And Shmuel added that as far as the river flows, there is the Land of Israel, implying up to the place where it pours into the Persian Gulf. b) The Torah referred to the inhabited land and not to the deserts; therefore the northern border goes from Hor Ha-har to the river Perat, between which and the core of the Land there are fertile territories that can be settled; but the part of the river Perat between which and the core of the Land there is a great desert is not considered the Land of Israel. And this fits the river Perat being the northern border and not the eastern border, and the eastern border is the great desert. And so it is implied that this is the view of Rabbi Avraham son of the Rambam in his commentary on Shemot 23:31, and so wrote the Kuzari 2:14, and Tosafot Yom Tov. And it seems that according to this opinion, the river Perat is the border as long as it flows from west to east, and when it begins to turn significantly southward, it already moves away from the Land of Israel. Within this opinion Rav Steiner has an explanation according to the Rambam (Tova Ha-aretz pp. 159-160), for it is implied from the Rambam that the border of the Land is a kind of square, for he wrote in Laws of Sanctification of the Month 11:17, regarding the sighting of the new moon, that it
Map of the eastern border, including a map of the Land of Israel according to the Rambam
[Map: The northern and eastern border according to those who hold that the Perat is the northern border] must be in the Land of Israel, and its place is up to a journey of six or seven days from Jerusalem, which is about three degrees of longitude from Jerusalem. But if we reckon only three degrees of longitude, we find that about a hundred km are still missing up to the river Perat, which is the border explained in the Torah. Therefore one must say that the measure of six or seven days is the range from which the witnesses can come, and one must bend the border line northward so that it extends to the river Perat.

sections.title_en: The Mitzvot Dependent on the Land
sections.body_en:
The Torah was given to Israel so that they would learn it and fulfil its mitzvot in the Land of Israel, for in the Land of Israel God's kingship and providence are revealed (as explained above 1:1-3). And so it is said: "For you are to pass over the Jordan to go in to possess the land which the Lord your God gives you, and you shall possess it and dwell in it. And you shall observe to do all the statutes and the judgements which I set before you this day. These are the statutes and the judgements which you shall observe to do in the land which the Lord, the God of your fathers, has given you to possess it, all the days that you live upon the earth" (Devarim 11:31-12:1). This implies that the obligation of the mitzvot is specifically in the Land. But on the other hand it is said (Devarim 11:16-18): "Take heed to yourselves, lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside and serve other gods and bow down to them. And the anger of the Lord be kindled against you… and you perish quickly from off the good land which the Lord gives you. (And even so, also when you are in exile) you shall lay up these My words in your heart and in your soul, and bind them for a sign upon your hand, and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes." So even in exile it is a mitzva to fulfil the mitzvot. The Sages explained that the mitzvot that are dependent on the Land, that is, connected to the soil, are a mitzva to fulfil only in the Land. But the mitzvot that are not dependent on the Land must be fulfilled in exile too, so that we will remember them and know how to fulfil them when we return to the Land. Moreover, through fulfilling them we will be aroused to repentance and merit to bring our redemption near (Yerushalmi Shevi'it 6:1; Kiddushin 1:8; Bavli Kiddushin 37a; Sifrei Ekev 43-44).

The mitzvot dependent on the Land are first and foremost the mitzvot concerning the whole of Israel: establishing the kingship or government according to the guidance of the Torah, including establishing an army according to the mitzvot of the Torah; establishing the Temple and the whole system of mitzvot connected to it, including the mitzvot of the kohanim and Levi'im, the cities of the Levi'im and the cities of refuge, plagues of houses, the beheaded heifer, eradicating idolatry and more; establishing the judicial system, at whose head is the Great Sanhedrin, whose role is to decide all the great and difficult questions. Likewise the Great Beit Din would sanctify the months and intercalate the years, and thereby set the times of the festivals of Israel. The mitzva of justice also requires appointing courts in every city, and beside them officers who enforce the law. Included in the mitzva of justice are the mitzvot connected to the procedures of the court, the deciding of the law and punishment. In order to appoint judges who have the authority to judge Torah law, their teachers must ordain them for this, so that they are ordained one from the mouth of another back to Moshe our teacher, who ordained the first sages. Only in the Land of Israel can the tradition of ordination be maintained. Indeed, even in the time of exile there is a mitzva to maintain a judicial system, but it is maintained by rabbis who are not ordained, and its existence is meant to preserve the Jewish community in loyalty to the tradition of Israel, without the vision of maintaining Torah justice in order to repair the world under the kingdom of the Almighty; therefore their authority concerns the common laws of damages and necessary deterrent punishment, and not uncommon laws, nor punishment meant to forge a holy people.

There is a further whole series of mitzvot that are dependent on the Land and connected to working the field and growing fruit, and these mitzvot are directed at every single individual of Israel. These are: orla, mixed seeds, mixed seeds of the vineyard, leket, shikheḥa, pe'ah, peret, olelot, bikkurim, terumot and ma'asrot, ḥalla, the first of the fleece, shevi'it and yovel. And although the principal obligation of these mitzvot is in the Land, the obligation of many of them extends to a certain extent outside the Land too (Peninei Halakha Kashrut 12:1, note 1).

sections.title_en: The Condition of the People Determines the Obligation of the Mitzvot
sections.body_en:
The obligation of the mitzvot dependent on the Land of Israel depends on the people of Israel dwelling in the Land. Let us set out briefly the history of the people of Israel in its Land and, in parallel, the order of the obligation of the mitzvot. After those who came up from Egypt conquered the Land and finished dividing it among the twelve tribes (in the year 2503 by the count we keep from the creation of the world), they became obligated in all the mitzvot dependent on the Land concerning the work of farmers, including terumot and ma'asrot, shevi'it and yovel. However, many more years passed until we succeeded in fulfilling the mitzvot connected to the whole of Israel, such as establishing the kingship, the Temple and the orderly judicial system, because for their fulfilment the people of Israel had to complete the settlement of the Land and become established in its inheritance. Meanwhile the temporary Mishkan stood in Shilo, and judges led Israel in a temporary way. After about four hundred years Shmuel the prophet arose to judge Israel, and by the power of his activity the judicial system was established, the kingdom of the house of David was founded, and the Temple in Jerusalem was built by King Shlomo, David's son (in the year 2929), and it stood for about four hundred and ten years.

About a hundred and forty years before the destruction of the First Temple, the king of Ashur exiled the tribes on the eastern bank of the Jordan and in the north of the Land, and from then the Torah obligation of the mitzvot of shevi'it and yovel lapsed, because the obligation of these mitzvot depends on all Israel being in its Land, each tribe in its inheritance; but they continued to fulfil them by instruction of the Sages. When all ten tribes were exiled, a situation arose in which most of Israel were no longer in their Land, and the Torah obligation of the mitzvot of terumot, ma'asrot and ḥalla lapsed, and they continued to fulfil them only by rabbinic decree. At the time of the destruction of the First Temple, the obligation of the public mitzvot dependent on the Land, such as shevi'it and yovel, terumot, ma'asrot and ḥalla, ceased altogether.

After seventy years of exile in Bavel the process of the Return to Tziyon and the building of the Second Temple began. Then the Great Assembly was established, which is the Great Beit Din of a hundred and twenty elders, among them several prophets, headed by Ezra the scribe. They instituted the order of sitting of the court, the wording of the blessings and prayers, and the order of prayer and Torah reading in the synagogues. They also sanctified the Land in order to renew the obligation to fulfil the mitzvot of shevi'it and terumot and ma'asrot. However, since most of the people were in exile, according to most poskim the obligation of these mitzvot then applied by rabbinic decree only (Peninei Halakha Kashrut 12:7).

Following the destruction of the Second Temple, in a gradual process that lasted hundreds of years, Jewish settlement in the Land dwindled more and more. Close to three hundred years after the destruction, the sages of the Land of Israel, headed by Hillel II, who was the Nasi, saw that they would not be able to continue maintaining the ordination of the sages and the court that sanctifies months and intercalates years, and they established that from then on the times of the months and festivals would be set according to the Hebrew calendar, which they sanctified for all generations; and since then all Israel conduct themselves according to the calendar (Peninei Halakha Zemanim 1:3; on restoring the laws to their former state, in halakha 21).

sections.title_en: The Different Borders of the Land Regarding the Obligation of the Mitzvot
sections.body_en:
The Land of Israel has three borders. The first is the whole Land, from the river of Egypt to the river Perat, and this is the border that determines the mitzva of settling the Land, which we learned about in halakhot 14-17.

The second, the 'border of those who came up from Egypt', is the borders that the twelve tribes inherited in the days of Moshe our teacher and Yehoshua bin Nun, the border of the inheritances on the western bank of the Jordan being mentioned in parashat 'Mas'ei', as we learned in halakhot 14-17. This border determines the place where the mitzvot dependent on the Land, such as terumot, ma'asrot and shevi'it, apply. However, as long as most of Israel are not in the Land, according to most poskim the obligation of the mitzvot of terumot and ma'asrot, ḥalla, shevi'it and yovel is rabbinic. The territories outside the 'border of those who came up from Egypt', although they are within the border of the complete Land of Israel, from the river of Egypt to the river Perat, did not become obligated in these mitzvot (Peninei Halakha Kashrut 12:2; 11; 14).

The third, the 'border of those who came up from Bavel', is the border of settlement of those who came up from Bavel in the days of the Second Temple, which is narrower than the 'border of those who came up from Egypt', and for it the Sages instituted their enactments and decrees, such as sefiḥin and demai. That is, both in the days of the Second Temple and after its destruction, the obligation of the mitzvot dependent on the Land applies to the whole 'border of those who came up from Egypt', but the enactments the Sages instituted were instituted only for the 'border of those who came up from Bavel', that is, for the places to which Jewish settlement spread in the days of the Second Temple. Today the obligation of the enactments applies to all the places under Israeli sovereignty (Peninei Halakha Kashrut 12:7-8; 17).

Syria: beyond the borders that Moshe and Yehoshua conquered, King David conquered Syria, including territories within the borders of the complete Land of Israel, such as Aram Damascus, and territories outside the borders of the Land, such as Aram Naharayim, between the Perat and the Ḥidekel. But since his conquest was meant to subdue enemies and not for the sake of settling the Land, his conquest is called an 'individual's conquest', and a doubt arose about the status of the territories of Syria regarding the mitzvot dependent on the Land. In practice it was ruled that by rabbinic decree the mitzvot dependent on the Land must be fulfilled there; however, the mitzva of settling the Land applies to all the territories of Syria within the area of the Land of Israel (ibid. 12:3, note 4).

sections.title_en: The Process of Restoring the Obligation of the Mitzvot
sections.body_en:
In order for us to return and fulfil the mitzvot of terumot, ma'asrot and ḥalla by Torah law, most of Israel must live in the Land. And in order for us to be obligated in shevi'it and yovel by Torah law, Israel must, in addition, dwell in the Land in their proper order (as explained in the next halakha).

The question is whom one must include in the Jewish people. Some say that the number of Jews today is about thirteen million, and in these years the number of Jews living in the Land is about to reach six and a half million Jews; consequently the first condition will be fulfilled, and we will be obligated in ḥalla and terumot and ma'asrot by Torah law. But their words are difficult, because the number thirteen million includes only the Jews who identify as Jews, and there are two more groups of Jews who are not identified as Jews but are Jews according to halakha. The first group is Jews whose parents assimilated in recent generations in the wake of the upheavals, persecutions and the Holocaust the Jewish people went through, whose Jewish identity can be clarified relatively easily. Together with them one may estimate that the Jewish people numbers between twenty and thirty million, and at the very least eighteen million.

The second group is much larger, and it includes all the descendants of the Jews who assimilated among the gentiles under the pressure of the terrible sufferings of exile, but who are Jews according to halakha, for they are descendants of Jewish mothers, and according to halakha whoever's mother is Jewish, even after a hundred generations, remains a Jew. And the Sages said, on the basis of the prophecies of redemption in the Torah, that in the future Eliyahu the prophet will come and return them to the source from which they were hewn (Mishna Eduyot 8:7; Rambam in his commentary on the Mishna). This group includes at the very least a hundred million and perhaps many more. For during the long exile, in all the wars and oppressions and terrible decrees of forced conversion, millions of Jews were removed from the bounds of Israel by force; and since the daughters always remain Jewish, one may estimate that all these anusim multiplied at the rate at which the nations among whom they assimilated multiplied. For example, it is estimated that the Jews who assimilated in Spain and Portugal were about ten percent of the whole population; it follows, then, that even today about ten percent of the inhabitants of Spain and Portugal, and likewise at least ten percent of the descendants of the Spaniards and Portuguese who emigrated to the lands of Latin America, such as Argentina, Brazil and Mexico, are Jews. The descendants of these anusim alone are at least thirty million Jews who were removed by force. Likewise some estimate that at least about ten percent of the population of Western Europe are descendants of Jewish anusim. And there are further descendants of Jews in the Arab lands, North Africa and Eastern Europe. It is possible that this group numbers a hundred million Jews and perhaps several hundred million. Likewise it is possible that one should add a third group, the descendants of the ten tribes, some of whom indeed returned and joined Israel, but many of whom remained in the lands of their exile (though according to opinions in Yevamot 17a their seed did not continue).

In practice it seems that at the very least one must add to the count of the Jewish people all those people whose parents assimilated in recent generations, for whom, by fairly easy clarifications, it can be proven through documents and testimonies that they are descendants of a Jewish mother. For according to halakha one cannot ignore what can be clarified relatively easily. However, regarding the members of the second group, who are the descendants of the anusim who assimilated among the gentiles throughout all the generations, there is room for doubt. One can say that although in the end all the dispersed will return to Israel, in the meantime they are not taken into account, but only those who can be proven with certainty to be Jews. And on the other hand, one can say that one must take into account everyone who is a Jew according to halakha, even if many generations have already passed since his family drew away from Israel. In practice it seems that a decision will be needed of a Great Beit Din which, by the authority of all Israel living in the Land, will decide the question of when the time will come at which we can say that most of the Jewish people lives in the Land. And perhaps we will have to wait for the appearance of a prophet who will guide us in this matter (Peninei Halakha Shevi'it Ve-yovel 11:3-4).

sections.title_en: Dividing the Land Among the Tribes
sections.body_en:
In order for us to return and fulfil the mitzvot of shevi'it and yovel by Torah law, it is not enough that most of Israel dwell in their Land; rather, they must dwell in their proper order, that is, every person of Israel must inherit his portion in the inheritance of his tribe (Arakhin 32b). For this purpose every person of Israel must again be assigned to his tribe and the inheritance of the tribes established anew (Rambam, Kings 12:3). From the prophecy of Yeḥezkel it emerges that even the location of the inheritance of the twelve tribes will change in the future, and each tribe will inherit a strip from the west to the east, with Dan in the north, and after him Asher, Naftali, Menashe, Efrayim, Reuven, Yehuda. Then the inheritance of the Nasi, in which are Jerusalem and the Temple, and in it there will also be an inheritance for the kohanim and the Levi'im. Then the division continues southward: Binyamin first, and after him Shimon, Yissakhar, Zevulun, up to Gad, who will be in the southernmost inheritance (Yeḥezkel 48; Bava Batra 122a). According to most commentators, the northern inheritance of Dan will reach near Turkey, at the source of the river Perat. Righteous converts too, who joined Israel while they were suffering, will receive an inheritance in the Land, each family of converts together with the members of the tribe they joined (Peninei Halakha Shevi'it Ve-yovel 11:5, note 4).

According to this, after the lineage of every person of Israel to his tribe is revealed and the Land is divided among the tribes, seemingly every person will have to move to live in the inheritance given to him among his tribe. And it seems in my humble opinion that the Great Beit Din together with the kingship will have the authority to divide the Land in such a way that every person of Israel will be able to remain living in his place or in a place he chooses, with a willingness to take part in continuing the heritage of the tribe within whose inheritance he lives. And if they go this way, perhaps they will need to establish that the more demand rises for the inheritance of a particular tribe, the more its territory will be divided into smaller inheritances that will suffice for everyone.

After the division of the inheritances, all Israel will be considered dwelling on their land in their proper order, and the Great Beit Din will begin to count the years anew, and we will be able to fulfil the mitzvot of shevi'it and yovel by Torah law (Peninei Halakha Shevi'it Ve-yovel 11:5).
